name: Zheng-Dao Bioelectric Neural Cipher Bridge
description:
The Neural Cipher Bridge is a subdermal implant that encodes all outgoing communications — voice, text relay, and data burst — through a biometric cipher generated by the user's own neural oscillation patterns. The cipher key is not stored anywhere. It is not transmitted. It exists only as a dynamic function of the user's living brain activity at the moment of transmission, reconstructed at the receiving end through a paired decoder that maps the sender's neural signature against a pre-registered baseline. Intercept a transmission from a Neural Cipher Bridge and you have noise. The key to decrypt it died the moment the user's brain state shifted — which is to say, constantly.

Zheng-Dao developed the Bridge from their existing neural-interface bioelectric research, adapting oscillation-mapping technology originally designed for medical monitoring into a communication security application. The implant is placed at the mastoid process, communicating via bone conduction to a secondary surface unit worn as an earpiece or embedded in a collar. The encoding process is invisible to the user — they speak, type, or transmit normally, and the Bridge handles cipher generation and application in the 0.006-second gap between neural signal origination and vocalization or device output.

The Bridge's primary limitation is pairing complexity. Establishing a new receiving decoder requires a 40-minute neural baseline mapping session conducted in person, using Zheng-Dao proprietary hardware. This makes it impractical for casual or one-off communication — it is a tool for established networks, long-term cells, and organizations that can afford the infrastructure of the pairing process. This limitation is, by some accounts, intentional: Zheng-Dao's licensing model generates ongoing revenue from baseline mapping sessions, and the friction of the pairing process keeps the Bridge in the hands of well-resourced users.

cultural_context: Among GLMZ's intelligence community — both corporate and independent — the Bridge carries a specific social weight. Having one means you have been vetted, baseline-mapped, and incorporated into a network that trusted you enough to invest 40 minutes of pairing infrastructure in you. It means someone believes your continued secure communication is worth the overhead. In some syndicate structures, receiving a Bridge is a formal initiation marker, equivalent in symbolic weight to a key or a seal. The pairing session itself has taken on ritual significance in some communities — a long, intimate process conducted in person, in a controlled environment, that functions as a kind of vow of operational alliance. Losing a Bridge implant — through surgical removal or death — requires the entire network to re-evaluate its pairing map.
known_users: High-value protected persons and their security coordinators
story_hooks: A dead operative's Bridge is still broadcasting — faint, degraded cipher fragments that no one should be able to produce from a dead brain. Either the body isn't as dead as reported, or someone has built something that shouldn't exist.

A player is offered a Bridge pairing by a contact they've worked with for months. The 40-minute session is intimate and vulnerable. Halfway through, the player realizes the baseline mapping equipment is also recording something else.
A network's decoder array has been stolen, meaning every Bridge-equipped operative in the cell is now communicating into a void — or into enemy hands, if the decoders have been cracked.

An 18-month baseline drift has gone uncalibrated in a key operative, and their transmissions are becoming increasingly incoherent at the decoder end. They don't know this. They think their messages are getting through.

Zheng-Dao's pairing clinic records — supposedly private and sealed — have surfaced on the information market, containing the neural baseline signatures of everyone who has ever been mapped. The implications for every Bridge network in the city are severe.
